lessons.title: Shock, Vibration, and Compression Forces in Transit
lessons.body: When your product leaves your workshop, it faces a gauntlet of physical forces. Shock is a sudden impact, like when a box is dropped or thrown. Vibration is continuous shaking, like a truck driving on a rough road. Compression is squeezing, like when boxes are stacked high in a container. In Africa, poor road conditions, manual handling, and long sea voyages make these forces intense. For example, a 20kg box dropped from 1 meter generates a shock of about 50 Gs. That's enough to crack electronics or break glass. Vibration from a typical truck at 50 km/h on a dirt road can cause screws to loosen or powders to settle and compact. Compression from stacking 5 boxes high can crush the bottom one if it's not strong enough. To protect your product, you need to understand these forces. Start by asking: How will my product be transported? By road, sea, or air? How many times will it be handled? Will it be stacked? Then, think about the weakest part of your product. A ceramic vase is fragile to shock; a liquid in a plastic bottle can leak under vibration; a cardboard box can collapse under compression. Simple tests at home can help. Drop a sample package from 1 meter onto concrete. Shake it vigorously for 5 minutes. Stack heavy books on it. See what happens. Record the results. This gives you a baseline. Then, design your packaging to absorb shock, dampen vibration, and resist compression. Use cushioning materials like foam, bubble wrap, or shredded paper. For compression, use strong double-wall or triple-wall corrugated boxes. For vibration, ensure the product is snug and doesn't move inside. Remember, the goal is to get your product to the customer in perfect condition, whether it's traveling to a nearby city or across the ocean.

lessons.title: Cushioning Design and Material Selection
lessons.body: Cushioning is the shock absorber for your product. It works by deforming slowly to absorb the energy of an impact, so your product doesn't have to. The key is to choose the right material and thickness for your product's weight and fragility. Common cushioning materials in Africa include foam (polyurethane or polyethylene), bubble wrap, air pillows, shredded paper, and corrugated cardboard inserts. For light items like a phone, 1 cm of bubble wrap may suffice. For a 10 kg ceramic pot, you might need 5 cm of closed-cell foam. The thickness depends on the drop height and the product's G-force tolerance. A simple rule: the more fragile the item, the thicker the cushion. But don't overdo itâtoo much cushioning can make the box too big, increasing shipping costs. Test different materials by dropping a packaged sample from 1 meter. If the product survives, you're on the right track. For vibration, materials like foam and bubble wrap also dampen shaking. But ensure the product is immobilizedâif it can move inside the box, it will rub and break. Use corner blocks or custom-cut foam to hold it in place. For compression, cushioning doesn't help much; you need a strong box. But cushioning can fill voids and prevent shifting that leads to compression damage. When selecting materials, consider cost and availability. Foam is expensive but reusable. Shredded paper is cheap but compacts over time. Bubble wrap is versatile but can pop. In Africa, you can source many materials locally: maize husks, banana leaves, or coconut fiber can be used as eco-friendly cushioning. However, they may not be as effective as engineered foams. Test them. A good cushioning design balances protection, cost, and weight. Remember, the goal is to protect your product without making the package too heavy or bulky.

lessons.title: Structural Design of Shipping Containers
lessons.body: The shipping containerâusually a corrugated boxâis your product's first line of defense. Its structure must withstand stacking, handling, and the elements. Corrugated boxes are rated by their bursting strength (Mullen test) or edge crush test (ECT). For export, you need at least a 32 ECT box for light items, and 48 ECT or higher for heavy or fragile goods. In Africa, many boxes are imported, but local manufacturers can produce them. When designing, consider the box's dimensions. It should fit your product snugly with room for cushioning. Too large, and the product shifts; too small, and it won't fit. The box style matters: a regular slotted container (RSC) is common and cheap, but for heavy items, a full overlap or double-wall box is better. For stacking strength, the vertical flutes of corrugated board provide compression resistance. But if the box is stacked on its side, strength drops. So mark boxes with

and arrows. Also, consider the environment: humidity can weaken corrugated board by up to 50%. In coastal areas or rainy seasons, use moisture-resistant coatings or plastic liners. For very heavy items, consider wooden crates. They are strong but heavy and may require fumigation for export. Plywood or OSB crates are lighter alternatives. When assembling, use the right tape: water-activated tape or hot melt glue for heavy boxes. Staples can tear. Test your box by stacking weights on it for 24 hours. If it bulges or collapses, reinforce it with corner boards or increase board grade. Remember, a well-designed box is not just about strengthâit's about cost, weight, and ease of handling. A box that's too heavy increases shipping costs; too light, and it fails. Find the balance.

lessons.title: Moisture and Humidity Control in Packaging
lessons.body: Moisture is a silent killer of exports. High humidity can cause mold, rust, and label peeling. In Africa, humidity varies from dry savanna to humid coastal regions. During sea transport, containers can experience humidity up to 90% and temperature swings that cause condensation. This is called container rainâwhen moisture condenses on the ceiling and drips onto your goods. To protect your product, you need to control moisture. First, dry your product before packing. For food items, ensure they are properly dried. For metals, apply a rust-preventive oil. Second, use moisture-absorbing materials like silica gel desiccants. For a 1 cubic meter box, use 500g to 1kg of silica gel, depending on humidity. Place desiccant sachets inside the package, not just on top. Third, use barrier packaging. Polyethylene bags or liners can block moisture. For sensitive electronics, use vacuum-sealed bags with desiccant. Fourth, consider the box itself. Corrugated board absorbs moisture. Wax-coated or plastic-lined boxes resist moisture better. You can also wrap the box in stretch film or use shrink wrap. For very sensitive items, use a desiccant breather or humidity indicator cards to monitor. When packing, avoid packing in humid conditions. If possible, pack in an air-conditioned room or during the dry season. For sea freight, use container desiccantsâlarge bags that hang in the container to absorb moisture. These are available from shipping suppliers. Also, ensure containers are in good conditionâno holes or leaks. If you're shipping in a shared container, your goods may be exposed to moisture from other cargo. So, always use your own moisture barrier. Test your packaging by placing a sample in a humid environment (like a bathroom) for a few days. Check for condensation or mold. A simple hygrometer can measure humidity. Keep it below 50% for most products. Remember, moisture damage is often not visible until it's too late. So, be proactive.

lessons.title: Barrier Packaging for Sensitive Products
lessons.body: Some products are extra sensitive: they need protection from oxygen, light, odors, or pests. Barrier packaging creates a shield. For example, coffee beans lose flavor when exposed to oxygen. Pharmaceuticals need protection from moisture and light. Electronics need protection from static and moisture. To create a barrier, you need materials with low permeability. Common barriers include: metallized films (like foil), EVOH (ethylene vinyl alcohol) films, and PVDC (polyvinylidene chloride) coatings. These are often used in flexible pouches or as liners in boxes. In Africa, you can find these materials from packaging suppliers in major cities. For small-scale exporters, a simple barrier is a high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bag with a twist tie, but it's not as effective as foil. For oxygen-sensitive products, use oxygen absorbers (iron-based sachets) inside a sealed barrier bag. For light-sensitive products, use opaque or amber-colored packaging. For odor-sensitive products, use activated carbon or zeolite sachets to absorb odors. For pest protection, use insect-resistant packaging or fumigation. When designing barrier packaging, consider the entire package: the product, the primary package (e.g., a pouch), and the secondary package (e.g., a box). Each layer adds protection. But each layer adds cost and weight. So, choose wisely. Test the barrier by storing a sample in a stressful environment. For example, put a coffee sample in a clear bag vs. a foil bag under sunlight for a week. Taste the difference. For moisture, use a hygrometer inside the package. For oxygen, use an oxygen indicator. Remember, barrier packaging is not just for food. Handmade cosmetics, natural remedies, and artisanal goods also benefit. For export, you must meet the importer's requirements. Some countries require specific barrier levels. So, communicate with your buyer. Also, consider sustainability: some barriers are not recyclable. But protection comes first. A damaged product is worse than a non-recyclable package.

lessons.title: Testing Protocols: Drop, Vibration, and Compression Tests
lessons.body: Testing your packaging is not optionalâit's essential. Without testing, you're guessing. You don't need a fancy lab. You can do simple tests at your workshop. Start with a drop test. Pick a sample package and drop it from 1 meter onto a hard surface (concrete). Drop it on each corner, edge, and face. That's 10 drops. Then inspect the product for damage. If it breaks, improve your cushioning. For vibration, place the package on a wooden platform and shake it vigorously for 5 minutes. You can use a mechanical shaker or just shake by hand. Or put it in the back of a truck and drive on a rough road for 30 minutes. Then check for loose parts or abrasion. For compression, stack boxes on top of each other. If you plan to stack 5 high, put 5 times the weight of one box on the bottom box. Leave it for 24 hours. Measure any deformation. If it crushes, use a stronger box or add internal supports. For moisture, place a package in a humid room (like a bathroom with hot shower) for 24 hours. Check for condensation or softening. For a more professional test, you can hire a testing lab in cities like Nairobi, Lagos, or Johannesburg. They can perform ISTA (International Safe Transit Association) tests. But for most small exporters, simple tests are enough. Document your tests: take photos, write notes. This helps you improve and also shows buyers you are serious. Also, test with the actual product, not a dummy. Because weight distribution matters. And test the full package: product, cushioning, and box. After testing, refine your design. Maybe add another layer of bubble wrap, or switch to a double-wall box. Remember, the goal is to simulate the worst-case scenario. If your package survives your tests, it will likely survive the journey. But always add a safety margin. Because real transit is often worse than your test.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Designing for Product Protection

For African exporters, packaging failure is rarely a technical curiosity â it is a direct loss of revenue, a damaged buyer relationship, and a reputational risk in markets where trust is hard-won. A single container of cocoa, cashew, coffee, cut flowers, or processed foods that arrives with compression damage, moisture spoilage, or broken units can wipe out the margin on the entire shipment. This practical reference lesson gives you the working knowledge to design packaging that survives the journey from farm gate or factory floor to a port in Europe, Asia, the Middle East, or intra-African markets.

The core principle is simple: packaging must protect the product against the forces and conditions it will actually encounter. That means understanding shock, vibration, compression, moisture, and barrier requirements â then selecting materials and structures that address them at the lowest total cost. Protection is not about maximum strength; it is about appropriate strength. Over-engineering wastes money and increases freight weight; under-engineering wastes product.

Shock, Vibration, and Compression Forces in Transit

Goods moving by road, rail, sea, and air experience three dominant mechanical forces. Shock â sudden impacts from drops, rough handling, or vehicle collisions â can exceed 50 g in severe cases. Vibration â continuous low-level oscillation from engines and road surfaces â causes abrasion, loosening, and fatigue failure over time. Compression â static and dynamic stacking loads â is the most common cause of pallet and carton failure in sea freight, where containers are stacked several units high for weeks.

In African export supply chains, these forces are amplified. Rural feeder roads are often unpaved and poorly maintained, subjecting goods to sustained vibration and impact before they even reach a port. Many exporters consolidate loads at inland depots, adding multiple handling cycles. Sea freight from Mombasa, Durban, Tema, or Lagos to European or Asian ports can take 20â40 days, during which compression and humidity act continuously on the load.

Cushioning Design and Material Selection

Cushioning absorbs energy and distributes impact over a longer time, reducing the peak force transmitted to the product. The key material property is the cushion curve â a plot of peak deceleration versus static loading for a given thickness. Common cushioning materials available in African markets include:

  • Expanded polyethylene (EPE) foam â good for repeated impacts, widely available in Kenya, South Africa, and Egypt.
  • Expanded polystyrene (EPS) â low cost, excellent for single-impact protection, but poor environmental profile and increasingly restricted in EU markets.
  • Molded pulp â made from recycled paper, locally producible, good for eggs, fruit, and small electronics.
  • Corrugated inserts and honeycomb â effective for edge protection and compression resistance.
  • Air pillows and paper void-fill â lightweight, suitable for e-commerce and small parcels.

Material selection must balance protection, cost, weight, availability, and destination-market regulations. The EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) is progressively restricting certain single-use plastics, so exporters targeting Europe should favor paper-based, molded pulp, or recyclable mono-material solutions.

Structural Design of Shipping Containers

Corrugated fibreboard boxes remain the workhorse of African export packaging. Their performance depends on flute type, board grade, and box construction. The McKee formula is the industry standard for estimating box compression strength:

BCT = 5.87 Ã ECT Ã â(caliper Ã perimeter)

where BCT is box compression test strength, ECT is edge crush test value, caliper is board thickness, and perimeter is the box perimeter. For humid sea freight, ECT values should be discounted by 30â50% because moisture softens fibreboard.

Table 1: Typical Corrugated Board Grades and Recommended Uses for African Exports
Board Grade ECT (kN/m) Typical Use Relative Cost
Single wall, C-flute4.5â5.5Light dry goods, small parcelsLow
Single wall, B-flute5.0â6.5Processed foods, cosmeticsLowâMedium
Double wall, BC-flute8.0â11.0Fresh produce, beverages, stacked sea freightMedium
Triple wall, AAA-flute13.0â16.0Heavy industrial goods, long sea voyagesHigh

Source: Fibre Box Association, Fibre Box Handbook (2020), and ISTA 3A/3E transit test protocols.

Moisture and Humidity Control in Packaging

Moisture is the silent killer of African export shipments. Relative humidity inside a sea container can exceed 90% for weeks, especially on routes crossing the tropics. Consequences include mould growth, caking of powders, corrosion of metal, softening of fibreboard, and loss of product quality.

Control strategies include:

  • Desiccants â silica gel or clay sachets sized to the container volume and voyage duration.
  • Moisture barrier liners â PE or aluminium-laminated container liners for hygroscopic cargo such as coffee, cocoa, and tea.
  • Ventilation â controlled airflow for fresh produce to prevent condensation.
  • Humidity indicators â cards or data loggers to verify conditions on arrival.

Barrier Packaging for Sensitive Products

Barrier packaging controls the transmission of oxygen, water vapour, light, and aroma. For African exporters of coffee, spices, nuts, dried fruit, and specialty foods, barrier performance directly determines shelf life and buyer acceptance.

Table 2: Barrier Properties of Common Packaging Films

Source: Adapted from Packaging Technology and Science data and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Small-Scale Food Processing guidance on packaging for developing economies.

WVTR = Water Vapour Transmission Rate; OTR = Oxygen Transmission Rate. Lower values indicate better barrier performance.

Testing Protocols: Drop, Vibration, and Compression Tests

Testing validates design before you commit to a full production run. The most relevant international protocols are:

  • ISTA 3A â parcel delivery system, small packages.
  • ISTA 3E â unitized loads of similar products (palletized).
  • ASTM D4169 â standard practice for performance testing of shipping containers.
  • ASTM D642 â compression test for shipping containers.
  • ASTM D999 â vibration testing of shipping containers.

For African exporters without access to full ISTA-certified labs, practical alternatives include in-house drop tests from specified heights, compression tests using calibrated weights, and road simulation by transporting sample loads on representative routes. Document everything â buyers increasingly ask for test evidence.

â  SAFETY WARNING:

Never use damaged, previously wet, or pest-infested packaging materials for export shipments. Contaminated wood packaging (including pallets and crates) can carry pests such as the Asian longhorn beetle and may be rejected or fumigated at destination under ISPM 15 rules â at your cost. Ensure all wood packaging is ISPM 15 heat-treated or fumigated and stamped. Reject any packaging that has been exposed to flood water, mould, or chemical contamination, as it can transfer hazards to food products and trigger regulatory rejection at EU, UK, US, or Gulf ports.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Identify the dominant transit hazards for your route (road quality, voyage duration, handling stages).
  2. Select board grade and box construction based on stacking height and voyage length, not just product weight.
  3. Apply a 30â50% compression strength discount for humid sea freight conditions.
  4. Use cushioning sized from cushion curves, not guesswork, for fragile or high-value items.
  5. Include desiccants or moisture barrier liners for hygroscopic products (coffee, cocoa, tea, spices, nuts).
  6. Match barrier film to product sensitivity â metallized or foil laminates for oxygen-sensitive goods.
  7. Run at least a drop, compression, and vibration test on a sample before full production.
  8. Verify ISPM 15 compliance for all wood packaging and document test results for buyers.

Further Reading

  • ISTA â International Safe Transit Association (free test protocol summaries and design guides)
  • FAO â Food and Agriculture Organization (free publications on packaging for small-scale food processors)
  • ASTM International (abstracts and scope of D4169, D642, D999 standards)
  • IPPC â International Plant Protection Convention (ISPM 15 wood packaging standard, free download)
  • International Trade Administration (USA) (free export packaging and logistics guides)

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills course Packaging for Export Markets. It is designed for agribusiness managers, processors, and exporter cooperatives seeking to reduce losses and meet international buyer requirements.

quiz.q: What is the primary difference between shock and vibration in transit?
options: A) Shock is continuous, vibration is sudden
B) Shock is sudden impact, vibration is continuous shaking
C) Shock only occurs in air transport, vibration only in sea transport
D) Shock is caused by stacking, vibration by dropping
quiz.explanation: Shock is a sudden impact like a drop, while vibration is continuous shaking like a truck on a rough road.

quiz.q: Which force is most responsible for crushing boxes at the bottom of a stack?
quiz.explanation: Compression is the squeezing force from stacking, which can crush the bottom boxes.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to test your packaging for shock resistance?
options: A) Drop it from 1 meter onto concrete
B) Soak it in water for 24 hours
C) Heat it in an oven
D) Stack heavy books on it for a week
quiz.explanation: A drop test from 1 meter simulates a typical handling impact.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a common cushioning material?
quiz.explanation: Steel rods are rigid and do not cushion; they would transmit shock.

quiz.q: What does the G-force in a drop test measure?
options: A) The weight of the package
B) The acceleration experienced during impact
C) The humidity inside the package
D) The compression strength of the box
quiz.explanation: G-force measures the acceleration of the impact, indicating how much force the product experiences.

quiz.q: Why is it important to immobilize the product inside its package?
options: B) To prevent movement that causes vibration damage
C) To make the package look neat
quiz.explanation: If the product can move, it may rub against the box and itself, causing abrasion or breakage.

quiz.q: Which material is a good eco-friendly cushioning option in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Maize husks are locally available and biodegradable, though they may compact over time.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum ECT for a heavy export box?
quiz.explanation: For heavy or fragile goods, a 48 ECT or higher box is recommended for adequate stacking strength.

quiz.q: What does RSC stand for in box design?
quiz.explanation: RSC is the most common corrugated box style, with flaps that meet in the middle.

quiz.q: How does humidity affect corrugated boxes?
options: B) It can weaken them by up to 50%
quiz.explanation: Moisture is absorbed by the paper fibers, reducing the box's compression strength significantly.

quiz.q: What is 'container rain'?
options: A) Rain leaking through container doors
B) Condensation forming on the ceiling and dripping
C) A type of vibration in sea transport
D) A method of cooling containers
quiz.explanation: Container rain occurs when warm, moist air condenses on the cooler ceiling of a shipping container and drips onto cargo.

quiz.q: Which desiccant is commonly used to absorb moisture in packaging?
quiz.explanation: Silica gel is a widely used desiccant that absorbs moisture from the air inside a package.

quiz.q: Where should desiccant sachets be placed?
options: A) Only on top of the product
B) Inside the package, distributed around the product
D) In the shipping container only
quiz.explanation: Desiccants should be inside the package to absorb moisture that enters or is trapped there.

quiz.q: What is a humidity indicator card used for?
options: B) To show if moisture has exceeded a safe level
quiz.explanation: These cards change color when humidity reaches a certain threshold, alerting you to moisture damage.

quiz.q: Which packaging material provides a good barrier against oxygen?
quiz.explanation: Metallized films, like foil, have low oxygen permeability and are used for oxygen-sensitive products.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an oxygen absorber in packaging?
options: B) To remove oxygen and prevent oxidation
quiz.explanation: Oxygen absorbers, often iron-based, chemically remove oxygen to prevent spoilage or flavor loss.

quiz.q: Which product would most benefit from light-blocking barrier packaging?
quiz.explanation: Pharmaceuticals can degrade when exposed to light, so opaque or amber packaging is used.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for vibration resistance?
options: A) Drop the package from 1 meter
B) Shake the package vigorously for 5 minutes
C) Stack heavy weights on it
quiz.explanation: Shaking simulates the continuous vibration experienced during transport.

quiz.q: In a compression test, if you plan to stack 5 boxes high, how much weight should you put on the bottom box?
options: A) The weight of one box
B) The weight of two boxes
C) The weight of four boxes
D) The weight of five boxes
quiz.explanation: The bottom box supports the weight of the four boxes above it, so you should apply four times the weight of one box.

quiz.q: What does ISTA stand for?
options: B) International Shipping and Transport Agency
C) Institute of Safety and Testing Analysis
D) International Standards for Transport and Assurance
quiz.explanation: ISTA is a nonprofit organization that develops testing protocols for packaged products.

quiz.q: Why is it important to document your packaging tests?
options: A) To show buyers you are serious about quality
C) To comply with tax laws
D) To make the package heavier
quiz.explanation: Documentation provides evidence of due diligence and helps you track improvements.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when testing packaging?
options: B) Testing only the box without cushioning
quiz.explanation: Testing only the box ignores the interaction between product, cushioning, and box.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of compression damage?
quiz.explanation: Compression causes the box to deform, bulge, or collapse under stacking weight.

quiz.q: What is the recommended humidity level for most products during storage?
quiz.explanation: Keeping humidity below 50% prevents mold, rust, and moisture damage for most goods.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used as a moisture barrier in packaging?
quiz.explanation: Polyethylene is a plastic that resists moisture transmission and is often used as a liner or bag.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a desiccant breather in a shipping container?
options: B) To absorb moisture from the air
quiz.explanation: Desiccant breathers are large bags that hang in containers to absorb excess moisture.

quiz.q: Which force is most likely to cause a screw to loosen in transit?
quiz.explanation: Continuous vibration can cause fasteners to gradually unscrew and loosen.

quiz.q: What is a good way to simulate real transit conditions in a simple test?
options: A) Put the package in a truck and drive on a rough road
B) Leave it in an air-conditioned room
C) Place it on a shelf
quiz.explanation: Driving on a rough road exposes the package to realistic vibration and shock.

quiz.q: Why should you test with the actual product?
options: A) Because dummy weights are not allowed
B) Because weight distribution and fragility matter
D) Because the product might be damaged anyway
quiz.explanation: The actual product's weight, shape, and fragility affect how forces are transmitted through the package.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of cushioning design?
options: A) To make the package look attractive
B) To absorb shock and protect the product
C) To reduce the weight of the package
D) To increase the size of the package
quiz.explanation: Cushioning deforms to absorb impact energy, reducing the shock transmitted to the product.
